synopsis: The booklet recommends a multi-fidelity, multi-tool architecture at every cost level rather than one universal simulator, because the market survey found no single tool with public evidence covering earth-moving automatic braking across many sites and all-weather sensing [f4968, f9321, f13071]. A four-month window, GPU-hour limits and coverage spanning 100-plus sites, 10-plus scenarios, weather and machine variants constrain full-fidelity testing; high-fidelity soil simulation runs 50–200 times slower than real time [f13548, f13606, f13605]. The proposed ladder combines millions of fast functional tests, medium-fidelity closed-loop regression, selected high-fidelity perception and soil cases, HIL for timing and interfaces, and targeted physical tests for correlation and final evidence [f9322, f9323, f9324, f9325, f9326, f9327]. Perception simulation should remain separate from braking simulation while supplying detection-delay, range and error distributions; machine-family braking models should likewise range from fast threshold models to selected high-fidelity edge cases [f6410, f13840]. Fidelity allocation must follow sensitivity and correlation work, with learned models used where held-out real-data evidence exists [f9328, f4971]. Modular tool chains require substantial integration work, which open standards reduce but do not eliminate; integrated suites reduce interfaces and support burden, and no independent evidence establishes a universal winner between integrated and modular architectures [f13240, f13609, f9359].
